source.title: The Sakk
source.summary: The medieval Islamic bill of exchange that became the modern cheque, and the trust networks that made it possible.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: In the 9th century, Baghdad's jahbadh bankers created a system where a piece of paper could move wealth across continents without a single gold coin traveling. The sakk, or bill of exchange, enabled the hawala trust network and mudaraba profit-sharing partnerships. Discover how this Islamic financial innovation became the English word "cheque" and laid the foundations for modern banking.

thread: A 9th-century Baghdad banker could write a piece of paper that moved gold across continents without a single coin traveling.
The jahbadh bankers of Baghdad created the sakk — a bill of exchange that let merchants cash money 4,000 miles away on reputation alone.
This trust network enabled the hawala system and mudaraba partnerships. Islamic finance moved wealth faster than armies could march.
We call it a "cheque" now, borrowing the Arabic word. Medieval Baghdad invented what we think is modern banking. https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-tt-2

linkedin.post: In 9th-century Baghdad, jahbadh bankers revolutionized commerce with a simple piece of paper called the sakk. This bill of exchange could move wealth across continents without a single gold coin traveling the route. The system relied entirely on trust networks — hawala systems and mudaraba partnerships that connected merchants from Spain to China. A trader in Baghdad could write a note that would be honored 4,000 miles away in Canton, purely on reputation. This wasn't just clever bookkeeping. It was the foundation of modern banking, created centuries before European banks existed. The word "cheque" comes directly from the Arabic "sakk." Medieval Islamic finance moved money faster than armies could march, enabling global trade on a scale that wouldn't be seen again for centuries. Listen: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-tt-2

upscrolled.post:
Baghdad's 9th-century bankers solved a problem that seems impossible: how do you move gold across continents without actually moving gold?

The jahbadh bankers created the sakk — a bill of exchange built on pure trust. A merchant could write a note that would be honored thousands of miles away, enabling global trade through hawala networks.

We call it a "cheque" now, borrowing their Arabic word and calling it innovation.
